**John Levendis and Sang H. Lee**

*Information Technology for Development* 19(1), 62–85, 2013

The impact of mobile and fixed telephones on economic growth has been the subject of increasing scrutiny in the literature on economic development. It is even of interest to theoretical macroeconomists, as it provides a useful test of the positive network externalities that should be present if endogenous growth theory is correct. We study the relationship between teledensity and growth in Asia, as the countries there have experienced wildly different levels of telephone penetration per capita, and of rates of growth of GDP per capita. We estimate several econometric models, one which explicitly treats telecom as strictly exogenous, and others which treat it as endogenous. Our conclusions are robust to the econometric specification. We find that the impact of teledensity on growth is positive, and increases with the level of telephone penetration. This provides support for endogenous growth theory.

[PDF](../files/levendis2013endogeneity.pdf) |
[DOI: 10.1080/02681102.2012.694793](https://doi.org/10.1080/02681102.2012.694793)

### Why This Research Matters

Does telecommunications cause economic growth, or does economic growth cause telecommunications investment? This chicken-and-egg problem — endogeneity — plagues nearly all research linking infrastructure to development. Most earlier studies assumed the answer was simple: phones cause growth, full stop. But if richer countries just buy more phones, the estimated effect of telecom on growth is biased upward.

Asia offers a compelling setting to test this. The continent spans enormous variation in both telephone penetration and growth rates — from near-zero teledensity in some countries to over 190 lines per 100 people in others, and from GDP contractions of 22% to booms above 30%. This variation gives econometric methods the leverage they need to separate cause from effect.

Beyond the policy question, the paper tests a prediction from endogenous growth theory: if telephone networks generate positive network externalities — each new connection making all existing connections more valuable — then the marginal impact of an additional phone line should *increase* with the level of penetration, not diminish. Neoclassical growth theory predicts the opposite: diminishing returns.

### What We Found

**Teledensity drives growth, and the effect gets stronger as penetration rises.** The coefficient on teledensity-squared is positive and statistically significant across nearly all specifications. This means each additional telephone line contributes more to growth than the last one did — evidence of increasing returns through network externalities, exactly as endogenous growth theory predicts.

**The results hold regardless of how you handle endogeneity.** We estimate models treating telecom as strictly exogenous (fixed effects) and as endogenous (one-step and two-step Arellano-Bond GMM). The positive, increasing relationship between teledensity and growth survives all three approaches and four different functional forms.

**The magnitudes are economically meaningful.** A 20-unit increase in teledensity — feasible based on what many Asian countries actually achieved between 2000 and 2006 — is associated with a growth-rate increase of up to roughly 2.5 percentage points, depending on the specification. At the upper end, that could cut the time to double a country's living standard from 36 years to about 16.

### How We Did It

We use panel data on 29 Asian countries and territories from 1981 to 2006 (World Bank data). Our preferred estimator is two-step difference GMM with Windmeijer-corrected standard errors, which addresses endogeneity by instrumenting current telecom levels with their own lagged values. Unlike prior work, we do not assume that non-telecom controls (trade, investment, government spending) are strictly exogenous either. Arellano-Bond tests confirm no problematic serial correlation, and Hansen J-tests validate the instruments across all specifications. We include a financial crisis dummy for 1997–1998 to absorb the Asian crisis shock.

### Implications

The finding of increasing returns has a direct policy implication: telecom investment becomes *more* valuable as penetration rises, not less. Countries should not expect diminishing payoffs as phone networks expand. But the paper also cautions against government-funded telecom subsidies — government spending itself has a large negative effect on growth in these models. The better path is lowering barriers to private investment: independent regulators, reduced licensing fees, and competitive entry.
